title: A new higher rate of income tax: 50% above £125,140
headline: Take the top rate back to 50%. Five times HMRC’s 1p row: about £1.2bn.
description: Raise the additional rate of income tax from 45% to 50% on income above £125,140, the rate that applied in 2010-11 to 2012-13. HMRC publishes the effect of a 1p change; this card takes five times that row, which is our extrapolation, not HMRC’s figure: HMRC says its ready reckoner is approximate beyond small changes, and the behavioural response embedded in the 1p row is the dominant term for this group. The same arithmetic is available on the taxes step as the additional-rate slider at +5p; adopting it here sets the same policy.

baselinePolicy.text: The additional rate has been 45% since 2013-14 (Finance Act 2012, section 1); it was 50% from 2010-11 to 2012-13. The £125,140 threshold is frozen to April 2031.
alreadyIncludes: Income tax thresholds frozen to April 2031 (Budget 2025, Table 4.1 line 46).

rawSource.note: Adopting this policy is five one-penny steps, so the unit is 0.2 of the toggle.

uprating.head: incomeTax
uprating.note: Shifted to the start year and scaled by the OBR March 2026 forecast for this receipts head (ADR-0004).

caveats: Five times HMRC’s published 1p row. HMRC says its ready reckoner is approximate beyond small changes, so this is our extrapolation and wears the assumption badge; nobody has certified a 50% rate.
HMRC’s estimate is for taxpayers on UK rates; income tax rates on non-savings, non-dividend income are devolved to Scotland.

considerations.text: The 1p row already carries HMRC’s behavioural response for this group, but HMRC warns the reckoner is approximate beyond small changes, and the 2010 to 2013 experience of a 50% rate is why the yield of a penny at the top is a fraction of the mechanical amount. A five-penny rise may raise less than five times a penny.

HMRC's figure is already net of the behavioural response, and for this group the response is the dominant term: the 2010 to 2013 experience of a 50% rate is the reason HMRC's published yield for a penny on the additional rate is a fraction of the mechanical amount.
Scotland sets its own rates on earned income, so a UK additional-rate change applies to taxpayers in England, Wales and Northern Ireland and to savings and dividend income everywhere.

interactions.text: This is the additional-rate slider at +5p. Setting both stacks two rate rises on the same income.
